Title: Can large language models estimate public opinion about global warming? An empirical assessment of algorithmic fidelity and bias

Survey Dataset: Ipsos KnowledgePanel, October 2017 (N = 1,304) and September 2021 (N = 1,006)
Survey Population: U.S. adults aged 18 and over
Application: Predicted variables:
- Beliefs about global warming (Yes/No/Don't know)
- Causes of global warming (Human activities/Natural changes/Both/Other)
- Worry about global warming (Not at all worried/Not very worried/Somewhat worried/Very worried)

- Psychological / personality covariates: issue involvement in global warming, interpersonal discussions about the topic, awareness of the scientific consensus
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy, F1, Macro-Average F1 (MAF1)

- LLMs can effectively reproduce presidential voting behaviors but not global warming opinions unless issue-relevant covariates are included.

- GPT-4 shows improved MAF1 scores when conditioned on both demographics and covariates.
- Algorithmic bias exists, particularly in underestimating Non-Hispanic Blacks' beliefs.
- Introduction of additional response options decreases accuracy.
- Conditioning with relevant covariates enhances algorithmic fidelity.

Results: Key Points: ChatGPT showed some ability to manipulate assessments but did not consistently outperform humans without coaching.
